titre: Oklo, the Nuclear Reactor Nobody Built
accroche: In 1972, a uranium-235 deficit measured at Pierrelatte reveals that a chain reaction took place in Gabon about 1.7 billion years ago.
contenu_vulgarise:
In May 1972, at Pierrelatte, in the Drôme department, a routine analysis of uranium yields a result that should not exist. Natural uranium generally contains 0.72% uranium-235, the rest being uranium-238. Samples from the Oklo deposit, in Gabon, contain only 0.60%, about 17% less. Other ores from the same site will later drop as low as 0.44%. The French Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) sets out to find where this uranium-235, the isotope power plants use as fuel, went.

## A Reactor With No Engineer

The answer comes down to one word: it was consumed by fission. This happened about 1.7 billion years ago (some sources round it to 2 billion). In the Oklo deposit, the reaction continued, on and off, for a few hundred thousand years, at sixteen sites made of patches of ore in centimeter-thick layers. Its power probably never exceeded 100 kilowatts thermal.

Two conditions are enough to explain it. The first is the concentration. Uranium-235 decays faster than uranium-238, so its share shrinks over time: when Oklo started up, it stood at about 3.1%, a value comparable to that of some modern reactors. The second is water. Groundwater played the role of moderator: it slowed the neutrons, which makes fission more likely. Oxygen was also needed, without which uranium does not dissolve in water.

## A Reactor That Breathes

In 2004, a team from Washington University in St. Louis reads the rhythm of this fission in the noble gases it left behind. The xenon and krypton isotopes, trapped in a phosphate from the deposit, bear the mark of pulsed operation: 30 minutes of activity, separated by 2.5 hours of rest. The concentrations of fission xenon and krypton, up to 0.03 cm³ per gram, are the highest ever measured in a natural material.

## What This Shifts

We file nuclear fission among human inventions: a reactor requires a design, a prepared fuel, a chosen moderator. At Oklo, all three came from geology alone, and they predated humanity by more than a billion years. The phenomenon itself cannot replay identically: today's natural uranium, at 0.72%, no longer reaches the concentration Oklo had at its disposal. The 0.12-point deficit, spotted in 1972 during a routine analysis, had stayed in the rock for 1.7 billion years.

repere.texte: The Oklo reactor operated in pulses of 30 minutes, separated by 2.5 hours of rest: this is what the isotopic composition of fission xenon and krypton trapped in a phosphate from the deposit reveals (Meshik, Hohenberg, and Pravdivtseva, 2004).
repere.source: Meshik, Hohenberg, and Pravdivtseva, Physical Review Letters 93, 182302 (October 27, 2004)

carte.punch: A nuclear reactor ran in Gabon, with nobody there, 1.7 billion years ago.
carte.idee: In 1972, a uranium-235 deficit (0.60% instead of 0.72%) measured at Pierrelatte reveals that a chain reaction took place at Oklo, in Gabon, about 1.7 billion years ago, in pulses of 30 minutes separated by 2.5 hours.
carte.source_courte: Meshik et al., Phys. Rev. Lett., 2004

quiz.question: Why was a natural chain reaction possible at Oklo 1.7 billion years ago, when it no longer is today?
choix: Because the Gabonese subsurface was then much hotter, which sped up fission
Because the rocks then contained another element, now vanished, that served as fuel
Because uranium-235 was more abundant there (about 3%) and groundwater slowed the neutrons
Because no water flowed through the deposit, which kept the reaction from stopping
quiz.explication: Uranium-235 decays faster than uranium-238: its share fell from about 3.1% to 0.72%, and the concentration condition is no longer met. Water is not an obstacle but a necessary moderator. No other fuel and no special heat is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the 2004 team discover that the Oklo reactor operated in pulses?
choix: By measuring the residual temperature of the deposit's rocks, still high in places
By reading the isotopic composition of fission xenon and krypton trapped in a phosphate from the deposit
By finding written records left by engineers who supposedly monitored the site
By comparing the site's current radioactivity with that measured at its discovery in 1972
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2004 team read, in the isotopic structure of fission xenon and krypton trapped in a phosphate from the deposit, a cycle of thirty minutes of activity separated by two and a half hours of rest.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What discrepancy was measured in May 1972 at Pierrelatte that triggered the investigation of Oklo?
choix: An excess of uranium-238, twice the concentration expected in a natural deposit
A trace of artificial plutonium, incompatible with a deposit several billion years old
A temperature anomaly in the processing furnaces, signaling a reaction still active
A uranium-235 deficit: 0.60% in the Oklo samples versus 0.72% expected
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Natural uranium generally contains 0.72% uranium-235. The Oklo samples contained only 0.60%, a deficit that led the CEA to look for where this uranium-235 had gone, and that led to the discovery of the reactor.
